## Purpose

This SOP describes procedures for recording weather and meteorological
conditions during field activities. Documenting weather conditions at
the time of sampling is essential for interpreting environmental data,
identifying storm-driven events, establishing baseline climate
conditions, and ensuring field safety. This SOP covers manual weather
observations, use of portable weather instruments, and deployment of
unattended data loggers for continuous monitoring [@wmo_guide2018].


## Scope

- **Applies to:** All EA Program field activities where weather
  conditions may affect data interpretation, sample quality, or
  personnel safety; deployment and retrieval of portable weather
  stations and data loggers
- **Does not apply to:** Climate modeling or historical meteorological
  analysis; operation of fixed, permanently installed weather stations
  managed by other departments; air quality monitoring (see
  [SOP-F502](SOP-F502-air-quality-portable-sensors.qmd))
- **Location:** All EA Program field sites


## Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                                          |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| PI / Field Lead   | Identify which weather variables are required for the
                      project; approve deployment of data loggers          |
| Trained Personnel | Record weather observations, deploy and retrieve
                      loggers, download data                               |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent use                |


## Definitions

- **Beaufort scale:** A standardized scale (0--12) relating wind
  speed to observable effects on land or water; allows wind speed
  estimation without instruments; developed by Admiral Beaufort
  in 1805 and adopted as the international standard by the WMO
  [@wmo_guide2018].
- **Cloud cover:** The fraction of the sky obscured by clouds,
  expressed in tenths (0--10) or oktas (0--8); recorded with each
  manual weather observation [@wmo_guide2018].
- **Dew point:** The temperature to which air must be cooled at
  constant pressure for condensation to occur; a direct measure of
  absolute humidity; can be derived from wet-bulb temperature
  measurements [@wmo_guide2018].
- **HOBOconnect:** The Onset smartphone app used to program and
  download data from Bluetooth-enabled MX-series HOBO loggers
  [@onset_hoboware].
- **Kestrel meter:** A handheld weather meter (Kestrel 3000 or
  similar) that simultaneously measures air temperature, relative
  humidity, wind speed, barometric pressure, and derived quantities
  (dew point, wet-bulb temperature, heat index); the standard
  portable weather instrument for EA Program field use.
- **Radiation shield:** A ventilated white housing that surrounds a
  temperature or humidity sensor to prevent direct solar radiation
  from inflating measured air temperatures; mandatory for any sensor
  exposed to sunlight [@wmo_guide2018].
- **Relative humidity (RH):** The ratio of actual water vapor
  pressure to saturation vapor pressure at the same temperature,
  expressed as a percentage; affects evapotranspiration, dew
  deposition, and physical and biological processes at field sites
  [@wmo_guide2018].
- **Screen height:** The standard height of 1.5 m above ground level
  for air temperature and humidity measurements; specified by the WMO
  to ensure comparability between stations and with published
  meteorological data [@wmo_guide2018].
- **Sling psychrometer:** A pair of wet-bulb and dry-bulb thermometers
  mounted on a frame that is swung to ventilate the sensors; used to
  determine relative humidity from the wet-bulb depression; a reliable
  low-cost alternative to electronic sensors.
- **WMO (World Meteorological Organization):** The United Nations
  agency responsible for international meteorological and hydrological
  standards; its Guide to Meteorological Instruments and Methods of
  Observation (WMO-No. 8) is the authoritative reference for field
  measurement practice [@wmo_guide2018].


## Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Lightning:** Cease all field activities and seek shelter in a
  vehicle or enclosed structure when lightning is observed. Wait at
  least 30 minutes after the last lightning strike before resuming.
- **Heat:** Southern California field sites can exceed 40 °C. Carry
  adequate water, take shade breaks, and monitor for heat-related
  illness.
- **Wind:** High winds can topple tripod-mounted instruments and
  create hazardous conditions near exposed ridgelines or water bodies.
- **Flooding:** Rapidly changing weather can cause flash flooding in
  Southern California canyons and channels. Monitor upstream conditions
  and have an evacuation route planned.
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Closed-toed shoes or field boots
- [ ] Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)

### Emergency Procedures

Refer to [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd).


## Equipment and Materials

| Item                                  | Notes                                    |
|:--------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Kestrel 3000 or equivalent meter      | For air temperature, RH, wind speed      |
| Sling psychrometer                    | Backup for RH measurement                |
| Rain gauge (manual graduated cylinder) | For precipitation measurement           |
| HOBO MX-series data logger            | For unattended monitoring per [SOP-F204](SOP-F204-hobo-weather-station.qmd) |
| Radiation shield (RS3 or similar)     | Required for any temperature sensor exposed to sunlight [@wmo_guide2018] |
| Compass                               | For wind direction measurement           |
| Field notebook                        | Per [SOP-F003](SOP-F003-field-notebook-protocols.qmd) |


## Procedure

### Manual Weather Observations

Record weather conditions at the start and end of each field session,
and at any time conditions change notably. Enter all observations in
the field notebook per
[SOP-F003](SOP-F003-field-notebook-protocols.qmd) [@wmo_guide2018].

| Variable                | Method                          | Units       |
|:------------------------|:--------------------------------|:------------|
| Air temperature         | Kestrel, sling psychrometer, or digital thermometer at 1.5 m in shade | °C |
| Relative humidity       | Kestrel or sling psychrometer   | %           |
| Wind speed              | Kestrel or Beaufort scale estimate | m/s or Beaufort number |
| Wind direction          | Compass bearing from which wind blows | degrees or cardinal direction |
| Cloud cover             | Visual estimate                 | Tenths (0--10) |
| Cloud type              | Identify dominant type          | Name (cumulus, cirrus, etc.) |
| Precipitation           | Observation and rain gauge      | mm; note type (rain, drizzle, none) |
| Barometric pressure     | Kestrel or smartphone app       | hPa         |

::: {.callout-tip}
### Tip
If you do not have a weather instrument, still record qualitative
observations. A note such as "clear sky, calm winds, warm" is far
better than no record. Note the source of any online weather data
(e.g., "NWS Ontario station, 08:00 reading").
:::

### Beaufort Wind Scale (Quick Reference)

| Beaufort | Description     | Speed (m/s) | Visual Indicator                |
|:---------|:----------------|:------------|:--------------------------------|
| 0        | Calm            | < 0.3       | Smoke rises vertically          |
| 1        | Light air       | 0.3--1.5    | Smoke drifts                    |
| 2        | Light breeze    | 1.6--3.3    | Leaves rustle                   |
| 3        | Gentle breeze   | 3.4--5.4    | Leaves and twigs in motion      |
| 4        | Moderate breeze | 5.5--7.9    | Small branches move; dust rises |
| 5        | Fresh breeze    | 8.0--10.7   | Small trees sway                |
| 6        | Strong breeze   | 10.8--13.8  | Large branches in motion        |

[@wmo_guide2018]

### Deploying Portable Data Loggers

1. Select a deployment location representative of site conditions and
   unlikely to be disturbed by people, animals, or flooding.
2. Mount temperature and humidity loggers inside a radiation shield
   at 1.5 m above ground per WMO screen height standards
   [@wmo_guide2018]. Secure to a tripod, post, or tree.
3. Mount rain gauges on a level surface with no overhead obstructions.
   The gauge orifice should be approximately 1 m above ground.
4. Program the logger using the HOBOconnect app or HOBOware software
   per [SOP-F204](SOP-F204-hobo-weather-station.qmd) [@onset_hoboware]:
   - Logging interval: typically 5 or 15 minutes
   - Start mode: delayed start
   - Time zone: Pacific Time
5. Record in the field notebook: logger serial number, GPS coordinates,
   deployment date and time, logging interval, sensor height.
6. Photograph the deployed logger with surrounding context.

### Retrieving Data from Loggers

1. Connect to the logger via Bluetooth (HOBOconnect) or USB cable
   [@onset_hoboware].
2. Download the data and save using the naming convention:
   `YYYY-MM-DD_SiteID_LoggerSN_weather.csv`
3. Do not clear the logger memory until you have verified the file
   contains the expected date range.
4. Upload the raw data file to the project GitHub repository under
   `data/weather/` within 48 hours.

### Using Online Weather Data

When on-site instruments are unavailable, supplement field observations
with data from nearby weather stations. Preferred sources for
Southern California:

| Source                | URL                                        |
|:----------------------|:-------------------------------------------|
| NWS                   | <https://www.weather.gov>                  |
| MesoWest / SynopticData | <https://synopticdata.com/mesowest>      |
| CIMIS                 | <https://cimis.water.ca.gov>               |
| Weather Underground   | <https://www.wunderground.com>             |

Record the station name, distance from field site, and retrieval date
in the field notebook and data file metadata.


## Quality Control

- Cross-check manually recorded air temperature against the nearest
  reliable weather station (NWS or CIMIS). Discrepancies greater than
  3 °C at similar elevation and time should be investigated
  [@wmo_guide2018].
- Inspect data loggers for drift by deploying two loggers side by side
  for at least 24 hours once per year. Temperature readings should
  agree within 0.5 °C; humidity within 5%.
- Check rain gauge calibration at least once per year by pouring a
  known volume of water through the gauge and comparing the logged
  total to the expected value.
- Flag any suspicious data (e.g., sudden temperature jumps, constant
  humidity at 100% for days) during data review and note the issue in
  the project data log.

## Training Record

Before recording weather observations or deploying loggers
independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP in full
2. Demonstrate correct use of a sling psychrometer or Kestrel meter
3. Demonstrate logger programming, deployment, and data download
   during a supervised field visit
4. Be signed off by the PI or field lead
